extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged readers, reformers, and those studying constitutions and rights (readers of Burke/Paine-era political pamphlets)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing what constitutes legitimate government, the origin and character of natural and civil rights, and the concrete elements a constitution must contain. Includes standards for historical argumentation and for practical constitutional design (electorate, representation, monopolies, election frequency, conflicts of interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine origin of equal rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The illuminating and divine principle of the equal rights of man (for it has its origin from the Maker of man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights should be traced to the creation of man rather than to intermediate historical precedents; if man has rights, they are inherent and universal. Use this as the foundation when arguing for natural rights rather than relying on contested antiquarian precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between natural and civil rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural rights appertain to man in right of his existence; civil rights appertain to man in right of his being a member of society. Every civil right grows out of a natural right (is a natural right exchanged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating laws, identify which rights individuals retain (those where execution power is equal to the right) and which are exchanged to society for collective enforcement (security/protection). Civil powers must be seen as aggregates of those exchanged natural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil power must not invade retained natural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The power produced from the aggregate of natural rights, imperfect in power in the individual, cannot be applied to invade the natural rights which are retained in the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional and legislative design must protect individual retained natural rights (e.g., intellectual rights, religion). Civil authorities' powers should be limited to functions for which individuals lack effective power.

rubrics_metrics.name: A constitution must be real and visible
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution is not a thing in name only, but in fact. Where it cannot be produced in a visible form, there is none. A constitution is antecedent to a government, and a government is only the creature of a constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate constitution should be expressible article by article: principles, organisation, powers, election modes, durations, and executive powers. If no concrete document exists, claim of a 'constitution' is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions must specify organisation and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution ... contains the principles on which the government shall be established, the manner in which it shall be organised, the powers it shall have, the mode of elections, the duration of Parliaments ... the powers which the executive part of the government shall have; and in fine, everything that relates to the complete organisation of a civil government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate constitutions by checking presence and clarity of these concrete elements (organisation, electoral method, durations, executive limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments must arise out of the people (social compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individuals themselves, each in his own personal and sovereign right, entered into a compact with each other to produce a government: and this is the only mode in which governments have a right to arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legitimacy by origin: governments founded by a compact among the people are legitimate; governments arising 'over the people' (by conquest or imposition) lack rightful foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of governments by origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments may be comprehended under three heads: First, Superstition; Secondly, Power; Thirdly, The common interest of society and the common rights of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to judge regimes: priestcraft/oracle-based (superstition), conqueror-based (power), or reason/common-rights-based. Prefer governments founded on common interest and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: A government cannot have the right to alter itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A government on the principles on which constitutional governments arising out of society are established, cannot have the right of altering itself. If it had, it would be arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For constitutional stability and anti-arbitrariness, changes to the constitution should be made by the nation (e.g., general convention), not unilaterally by the current government or parliament claiming self-amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and method of constitutional reform belongs to the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of reform is in the nation in its original character, and the constitutional method would be by a general convention elected for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reforming a constitution, prefer an inclusive, representative convention rather than internal self-reform by sitting authorities; avoid paradox of vitiated bodies reforming themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral qualification: broad and consistent franchise
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of France says that every man who pays a tax of sixty sous per annum ... is an elector. This is contrasted with the capricious and limited English qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate elector qualifications for fairness: favour clear, modest, and widely inclusive criteria rather than arbitrary, patchwork, or monopoly-based qualifications that exclude the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should be proportional to population/taxable inhabitants
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that the number of representatives for any place shall be in a ratio to the number of taxable inhabitants or electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge representative systems by proportionality; rotten boroughs or unequal representation (tiny places sending same members as huge counties) violate the principle of fair representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent and regular elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that the National Assembly shall be elected every two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, relatively frequent elections are a constitutional safeguard against entrenchment; long or arbitrarily-extended terms indicate lack of true constitutional restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: No monopolies; free trades and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be no monopolies of any kind -- that all trades shall be free and every man free to follow any occupation by which he can procure an honest livelihood, and in any place, town, or city throughout the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional or legal frameworks should avoid chartered monopolies and barriers to mobility; permit free choice of lawful occupation and remove artificial privileges that bind markets or citizenship by locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: No game laws that privilege owners against common rights
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be no game laws, that the farmer on whose lands wild game shall be found ... shall have a right to what he can take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should avoid legal privileges (e.g., exclusive game laws) that place private property or leisure above the natural rights of those who actually provide or tend the land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent conflicts of interest: no placemen or pensioners in assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve the national representation from being corrupt, no member of the National Assembly shall be an officer of the government, a placeman or a pensioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disqualify those with executive office, state-dependent pay, or patronage ties from legislative bodies to reduce corruption and preserve independent representation (anti-pattern: 'loaves and fishes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical reasoning must start from established facts and causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Before anything can be reasoned upon to a conclusion, certain facts, principles, or data, to reason from, must be established, admitted, or denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical or political argumentation, establish causes and facts first. Avoid presenting consequences without investigating causes (criticises Burke for exhibiting consequences without their causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dramatic licence and omission in historical accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Burke ... has taken poetical liberties of omitting some facts, distorting others, and making the whole machinery bend to produce a stage effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good historical/political writing should not omit relevant incidents (e.g., Garde du Corps cockade incident), invent lurid details (e.g., bishops to the lamp-post) or reshape events merely for theatrical effect. Provide evidence and avoid conjectural dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace rights and institutions to their true origin rather than intermediate precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: The error of those who reason by precedents drawn from antiquity ... is that they do not go far enough into antiquity. ... if antiquity is to be authority, a thousand such authorities may be produced, successively contradicting each other; but ... we shall at last come to the time when man came from the hand of his Maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justifying rights or institutions, avoid selective appeal to historical precedents; prefer grounding in fundamental origins or first principles where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergenerational equality of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Every generation is equal in rights to generations which preceded it, by the same rule that every individual is born equal in rights with his contemporary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional claims or entitlements should recognise that posterity holds rights equal to current generations; no generation may validly impose perpetual government that extinguishes later generations' equal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental duties: duty to God and neighbour
rubrics_metrics.description: His duty to God, which every man must feel; and with respect to his neighbor, to do as he would be done by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral considerations underpin civil society; governments and citizens should be judged partly by whether they cultivate moral duties and mutual respect in civic life.
